soil-found-090.title: Soil science: one resource, many disciplines
soil-found-090.text: Engineers, agronomists, chemists, geologists, ecologists, microbiologists, archaeologists and planners all add to what is known about soils. Soil science gathers that knowledge into the study of soil as a natural resource. It asks how soil forms and how it is classified and mapped. It measures soil's physical, chemical, biological and fertility properties, and asks how they bear on its use and management. The field has two main historical branches. {{ref:soil-found-095}} studies soil in its natural setting. {{ref:soil-found-097}} studies soil in relation to the uses that depend on it. Both draw on the physics, chemistry and biology of soil. Soil occupies {{ref:soil-found-084}}, one of the spheres the geosciences use to organize the Earth. Climate change, {{ref:soil-phys-246}} and {{ref:soil-env-212}} now drive much new research, along with interest in biodiversity and in past cultures. Soil scientists also worry about preserving soil and farmland as population and food consumption grow and more land is degraded. Mapping, which classifies the soils of an area and geo-encodes them, increasingly relies on digital methods and remote sensing. In 1998 a new international system, {{ref:soil-class-016}}, replaced the older one from the FAO. Its current 4th edition dates from 2022.

soil-found-033.title: Phyllosilicates: minerals built in stacked sheets
soil-found-033.text: Some minerals split into thin, flexible flakes. These are the phyllosilicates, or sheet silicates, made of sheets of linked silica tetrahedra. The class includes {{ref:soil-chem-135}} and the minerals at the heart of {{ref:soil-found-040}}. Each tetrahedron is bound to its neighbors at three oxygen sites, giving a silicon to oxygen ratio of 2:5. That leaves the tetrahedral sheet negatively charged, and a sheet of octahedra balances it. These tetrahedral (T) and octahedral (O) sheets stack into layers, and the stacking defines the groups. In 1:1 minerals, T-O stacks are held together by hydrogen bonds. In 2:1 minerals, T-O-T stacks are held by weaker forces, described in {{ref:soil-chem-227}}. This peeling mineral is also a T-O-T stack, with a difference. It puts aluminum in the tetrahedral sheets, whereas the 1:1 and 2:1 minerals hold Al3+ in the octahedral sites. Metal ions bond its layers together, making them harder. Because the bonds between layers are weak, phyllosilicates show a prominent basal cleavage, a tendency to split along flat planes. Octahedral sheets come in two kinds. When every site is filled they are trioctahedral. When some sites are empty, as in pyrophyllite, they are dioctahedral.

soil-chem-199.title: Zeolites, the mineral sponges that swap ions
soil-chem-199.text: Some minerals behave like sponges built by a chemist. Zeolites are a group of crystalline minerals of the kind described in {{ref:soil-chem-223}}, a family of {{ref:soil-found-031}} riddled with microscopic pores. They are widely used to catch other substances on their surfaces and to speed up reactions as catalysts. Their frameworks carry negatively charged aluminium centres. Positive ions must sit beside them, and these can be swapped for others, so zeolites exchange ions. Over 40 natural frameworks are known among 253 identified by December 2018. Altered {{ref:soil-chem-200}} has formed zeolite deposits. Yet much material sold as zeolite is ground volcanic tuff holding little of it, used for building stone, aggregate, cement and products that improve soil.

soil-chem-241.title: Phosphate minerals and where soil phosphorus goes
soil-chem-241.text: Phosphate forms over 300 minerals. The commonest pure primary ones are the apatites, Ca5(PO4)3(F,Cl,OH), with fluor-, chlor- and hydroxyapatite as the end members. Rock phosphate is mined for fertilizer. Soils typically hold 400-800 mg of phosphorus per kg, against a crustal average of 1050 mg per kg. Phosphate in soil, whether from rock or fertilizer, precipitates with calcium, aluminium and iron. Wet, sub-oxic soils form iron phosphates such as vivianite and {{ref:soil-chem-234}}. Acidic soils form aluminium phosphate, as in variscite. Soils described in {{ref:soil-chem-035}} form calcium phosphates such as brushite, which commonly precipitates where fertilizer is banded at high concentration.

soil-chem-120.title: Redoximorphic features: colors that record wet and dry
soil-chem-120.text: Soil keeps a diary of its wetness in color. Redoximorphic features are color patterns from the loss or gain of pigment against the matrix color. They form by oxidation and reduction of iron or manganese and their movement, or a matrix color is set by ferrous iron. A pattern counts as redoximorphic only once the processes that formed it are known or inferred. Reducing conditions give disrupted color with complex mottled patterns and points of color concentration, whereas aerobic conditions give uniform or gradual changes. As a wet soil dries and oxygen returns, reduced iron can re-oxidize locally into bright yellow-brown mottles. Fluctuating water levels give red and yellow blotches mixed with gray. Continuous strong reduction from long-term waterlogging gives gleyed conditions in dark gray to blue to black. Eh, the voltage measured in a soil, expresses the potential for these reactions. Classification uses the features: {{ref:soil-class-106}} soils with {{ref:soil-class-155}} and redoximorphic features are Aquerts, and the WRB suffix σ marks permanent saturation without them. They provide critical information for soil interpretation. See also {{ref:soil-chem-118}}, {{ref:soil-found-025}} and {{ref:soil-found-028}}.

soil-bio-271.title: Fungi: the threads that decompose and partner
soil-bio-271.text: Most fungi grow as thread-like hyphae 2 to 10 micrometres across and up to several centimetres long. They extend at their tips and branch, and their high surface-to-volume ratio suits nutrient extraction and invading substrates. Fungi are more closely related to animals than to plants, though they were once classed as plants for their immobile lifestyle. Along with bacteria they are the major decomposers in most terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems, so they are central to food webs and to the cycling of elements covered in {{ref:soil-fert-140}}. They also partner with other life; see {{ref:soil-bio-226}}. Over 90% of plant species form mycorrhizal relationships with fungi and depend on them for survival, a symbiosis that dates back at least 400 million years. Lichens pair a fungus with photosynthetic algae or cyanobacteria, and some ants cultivate fungi for food and nest structure. Many fungi are plant parasites, such as the rice blast fungus and those causing Dutch elm disease and chestnut blight. As of 2019 nine major lineages are recognised, including Chytridiomycota, {{ref:soil-bio-177}}, Ascomycota and Basidiomycota. The last two form the species-rich Dikarya, with all mushrooms and most plant pathogens.

soil-bio-274.title: Protozoa: single cells that eat bacteria
soil-bio-274.text: Protozoa are single-celled eukaryotes, free-living or parasitic, that feed on organic matter such as other microorganisms or debris. The name is now used loosely for heterotrophic single-celled protists, since Protozoa as a taxon is not monophyletic. Classic examples are Amoeba, Paramecium and Euglena. They range from about 1 micrometre to several millimetres, and are flagellates, ciliates or amoebae according to how they move. All need a moist habitat, but many survive dry spells as resting cysts; they are common in soils and mosses. All are heterotrophs, engulfing prey by phagocytosis or taking up dissolved matter by osmotrophy, and some are mixotrophs hosting symbiotic algae. Most reproduce asexually by binary or multiple fission; sexual exchange is generally decoupled from reproduction. In the microbial food web they are the most important consumers of bacteria and mobilise nutrients, passing bacterial and algal production on and solubilising nutrients held in {{ref:soil-bio-269}}. Termite gut flagellates help their host digest wood by breaking down complex sugars. See also {{ref:soil-bio-014}} and {{ref:soil-bio-271}}.

soil-bio-081.title: Dwarf forests, where poor soil grows miniature trees
soil-bio-081.text: On Mount Hamiguitan in the Philippines, 6,834 hectares of forest grow in miniature. It is the largest known pygmy forest in the country and possibly the world. A dwarf forest, also called an elfin or pygmy forest, is an uncommon ecosystem of small trees, home to small animals such as rodents and lizards. Most grow at high elevations, where the air is humid but the soil is poor. The two main types are coastal temperate and montane tropical. In tropical mountains the trees reach only 5–8 m, with shallow roots and abundant plants that grow perched on other plants. High winds largely set their height.

soil-form-172.title: Hydrolysis: how water cracks minerals open
soil-form-172.text: Water does more than wet a mineral; it can break it. Hydrolysis is any chemical reaction in which a water molecule breaks one or more chemical bonds. One fragment of the split molecule gains a hydrogen ion and the other gains a hydroxide. It is the reverse of condensation, which joins molecules by removing water. The lab manual says all minerals weather this way, and that hydrolysis is the primary reaction releasing most plant nutrient elements from minerals. In one example, {{ref:soil-form-143}} and water yield an aluminum silicate, K+ and OH-. This is a main route of {{ref:soil-found-058}}. Hydrolysis also drives {{ref:soil-chem-076}}. Metal ions in water form aqua ions that act as acids: trivalent Al3+ and Fe3+ are weak acids with a pKa comparable to acetic acid, while Na+ hydrolyses almost imperceptibly. In the soils of {{ref:soil-chem-030}}, loosely bound Al3+ and Fe3+ and sparingly soluble sulfates such as jarosite release H+ this way. In the soils of {{ref:soil-chem-019}} the carbonate anion hydrolyses to bicarbonate and hydroxyl ions, raising pH. The enzyme {{ref:soil-fert-224}} catalyzes the hydrolysis of {{ref:soil-fert-021}}, and highly alkaline soils, pH about 8.2 or higher, increase it.

soil-bio-055.title: The enzymatic latch that holds decay in check
soil-bio-055.text: In {{ref:soil-class-070}}, one family of enzymes holds the key to decay. The enzymatic latch is the control of breakdown in this waterlogged material by phenol oxidases. Phenolic compounds inhibit the hydrolase enzymes that digest dead material. Phenol oxidases destroy those phenolics and so release decay, which means limits on the microbes limit breakdown. Saprotrophic bacteria release microbial extracellular enzymes (MEEs) when their energy and nutrient needs are unmet, so MEEs signal nutrient availability. Several tell a story. One, {{ref:soil-bio-257}}, releases sugars that give microbes energy and easily used carbon. Acid and alkaline forms of the enzyme described in {{ref:soil-fert-275}} show the potential to free phosphorus from organic forms. Phenol oxidases can also degrade or detoxify aromatic pollutants into carbon sources.

soil-bio-278.title: Free-living bacteria that fix nitrogen
soil-bio-278.text: Plants and animals cannot use nitrogen gas, or nitrogen locked in organic molecules. It must be converted to ammonium and nitrate, a bacterial process called nitrogen mineralization. Some free-living soil bacteria take nitrogen gas from the air and turn it into a form plants can use to make amino acids and proteins. {{ref:soil-bio-237}} and Azotobacter are free-living fixers, and it attaches to root surfaces and makes substances that help plants tolerate stress. They add only modest nitrogen, but it matters in natural systems where nutrient cycling is efficient. {{ref:soil-bio-178}} in swellings on legume roots do far more, receiving sugars from the plant and supplying usable nitrogen. An alfalfa stand may fix hundreds of pounds per acre a year, peas about 30 to 50. All of these are {{ref:soil-bio-002}} working alongside {{ref:soil-bio-003}}.

soil-form-141.title: Feldspar: the rock mineral that becomes clay
soil-form-141.text: Feldspars make up about 60% of the Earth's crust and 41% of the continental crust by weight. They are rock-forming aluminium tectosilicate minerals that also contain cations such as sodium, calcium, potassium or barium. The commonest are the sodium-calcium plagioclase feldspars and the potassium-sodium alkali feldspars. Formed at high temperature, they are unstable at the surface, especially plagioclase, so they weather easily. Hydrolysis, described in {{ref:soil-form-172}}, turns them into {{ref:soil-chem-079}} including {{ref:soil-chem-094}}, {{ref:soil-chem-091}} and {{ref:soil-chem-088}}, and because feldspars are so abundant, clays are abundant too. Clay-replaced feldspar looks chalky beside glassy unweathered grains. Feldspar-rich sediment therefore points to little chemical weathering before burial.

soil-form-034.title: Cryoturbation: how frost churns the ground
soil-form-034.text: In the frozen north, the soil mixes itself. Cryoturbation is frost churning: the mixing of material from different soil horizons, down to bedrock, by repeated freezing and thawing in soils with permanently frozen ground. It occurs to some degree in most soils of the order {{ref:soil-class-096}}, whose name comes from Latin gelare, to freeze. Autumn freezing forms wedges of ice, described in {{ref:soil-form-036}}, in the most erodible parts of the parent rock. In summer the {{ref:soil-env-146}} lets loosened material move both down and up. Moisture moves from the warm surface to the cold top of the frozen layer, drying the upper soil into a granular structure with lens-shaped bodies of ice. These lenses grow by drawing unfrozen water along a thermal gradient, displacing and mixing mineral and organic material at the ice-water interface. Separation of coarse from fine material produces {{ref:soil-phys-163}}. Cryoturbation is the dominant force in that layer and tends to make it uniform in composition. It is strongest on exposed sites and weak in sheltered valleys: Turbels show it in over one-third of that layer, with distorted {{ref:soil-form-005}}, Orthels in less. In {{ref:soil-phys-160}} it can bring base-rich water to the surface, neutralizing acidity and replenishing nutrients. In effect, ice scrambles the layers described in {{ref:soil-found-001}}.

soil-fert-274.title: Managing soils overloaded with phosphorus
soil-fert-274.text: A survey found the average US dairy herd was fed about 25 percent more P than the National Research Council recommends. High-P soils result from excessive P fertilizer or, more often, heavy manure use ({{ref:soil-fert-254}}), and they need managing to limit phosphorus loss to water. They are common on livestock farms with limited land and imported feed, where feed nutrients exceed those exported in animal products and where manure or compost applied to meet N adds extra P. The extra supplemental P can cost thousands of dollars for a 100-cow herd and ends up as a potential pollutant. Risk depends on context. Sites near critical water with slope, fine texture, poor structure or poor drainage need aggressive measures, while flat, grass-bordered vegetable or urban plots pose far less. First cut P in animal diets, then stop extra P by spreading manure on more land, swapping fields, or using legume covers and forages for N. Do not use a high-P source such as compost to supply N, since P builds up over the long term. Reduce runoff and erosion with reduced tillage, contour strips, cover crops, {{ref:soil-water-109}} and buffers. Tile drainage can still carry P, especially after heavy liquid manure. Soil-test P falls slowly once imports stop, so test every two to three years. A one-time tillage can redistribute P built up at the surface of no-till soil, followed by starter P and injected manure.

soil-agri-204.title: Erosion's damage beyond the farm
soil-agri-204.text: Sediment is the number one contaminant of most waters worldwide, and it often carries nutrients, pesticides and other chemicals. Soil carried off fields fills streams, rivers, reservoirs and estuaries, and blowing dust reaches towns. Off-site costs to fisheries, recreation and industry can exceed the lost farm productivity. So soil loss below T may be tolerable for yields but not for water and air quality. Clay-rich soils are especially troublesome. Their particles stay suspended as colloids in runoff, do not settle in ponds or {{ref:soil-agri-160}}, and travel far with nutrients and pesticides. Clay and silt suspended in the air also travel long distances and can cause respiratory problems. This is the downstream side of {{ref:soil-water-001}}.

soil-form-159.title: Reading runoff from slope and texture
soil-form-159.text: How fast will rain run off a field? Percent slope is rise over run times 100, read directly with an Abney level or clinometer held parallel to the slope. Runoff rises with slope and falls with infiltration rate. Granular, porous soils shed less water than massive, low-porosity ones, because more water infiltrates. A moister soil saturates sooner and so runs off sooner, while plant cover intercepts raindrops and reduces erosion. In the field table, slopes of 0-1% give very slow runoff for all textures, 6-12% gives rapid runoff for {{ref:soil-phys-012}} textures but very rapid for clays, and over 18% is very rapid for all textures.

soil-form-162.title: Soils of British Columbia and Yukon
soil-form-162.text: No other part of Canada has soils as varied as British Columbia and Yukon, thanks to a varied geologic history, rugged terrain and a wide climate range. The region holds all ten soil orders of the Canadian system. {{ref:soil-class-138}} soils have the largest extent in British Columbia, on {{ref:soil-chem-004}} under cool, humid conditions, and Luvisols are the other dominant order, on loamy glacial tills in the Interior plateaus and boreal forest. Cryosols occur in permafrost areas of northern Yukon and on high mountain peaks, while {{ref:soil-class-123}} soils occur only in the arid Central Interior. {{ref:soil-class-139}} soils mark landslide-prone and avalanche-prone slopes and the Fraser Delta, and drained {{ref:soil-class-127}} soils in the Fraser Valley are among the province's most productive farm soils. Mining leaves {{ref:soil-class-044}}; in metal mining the chief concern is acid rock drainage, because sulphide minerals such as {{ref:soil-chem-134}} weather rapidly to sulfuric acid.

soil-form-167.title: Soils of Quebec
soil-form-167.text: Quebec's soils sit in bands from south to north, and there are seven soil orders in them. They formed over the last 6,000 to 10,000 years, after the Laurentide Ice Sheet retreated, on parent materials that follow the Canadian Shield, the Appalachians and the sedimentary St. Lawrence valley. Podzols cover 39% of Quebec, Brunisols 17% and Organic soils 8%. Dystric Brunisols can turn into Podzols over several thousand years, as on the North Shore. After glaciation the Champlain Sea left salt-rich clay in the St. Lawrence Lowlands; leaching of the salt and river incision made it unstable, causing over 700 landslides and {{ref:soil-water-101}}. Only a small area has high agricultural potential: Canada Land Inventory Classes 1 to 3 total about 0.28 ha per Quebecer, the smallest of any province, and about 80% of them are cropland, so conserving them matters.

soil-found-058.title: Chemical weathering: rock remade for life at the surface
soil-found-058.text: Most rock is born hot and squeezed. It forms at high temperature and pressure, so its minerals are often unstable in the cool, wet, oxidizing conditions at the Earth's surface. Chemical weathering is the result. Water, oxygen, carbon dioxide and other substances react with rock and change its composition. It does three things at once. It turns some of the minerals the rock formed with, covered in {{ref:soil-form-140}}, into new minerals, of the kind described in {{ref:soil-chem-235}}. It carries other substances off in solution. And it leaves the most stable minerals unchanged, as a resistate. Water is the main agent. Through the reactions in {{ref:soil-found-060}}, it turns many of these original minerals into fine sheet minerals or hydrated oxides. Oxygen oxidizes minerals, and carbon dioxide drives carbonation. The new set of minerals sits closer to equilibrium with surface conditions. True equilibrium is rare, though, because water keeps washing the dissolved products away. Chemical weathering is usually much more important than the mechanical kind in {{ref:soil-found-053}}. Mountains show its reach. Uplift exposes fresh rock to air and moisture, releasing calcium and other ions into surface waters.

soil-phys-004.title: Aggregate stability: will the crumbs hold together?
soil-phys-004.text: A soil can look healthy and still fall apart in the first hard rain. Soil aggregate stability measures how well aggregates resist breaking apart under forces such as water and wind erosion, shrinking and swelling, and tillage. It describes {{ref:soil-phys-001}}, responds to management and serves as a soil-quality indicator because it combines physical, chemical and biological properties. It directly controls pore-size distribution, and through it water retention, water movement and air movement. Well-aggregated soil holds a mix of pore sizes: micropores retain and store water, while mesopores and larger pores let water and air move in. Such soil usually takes in water faster and is not prone to ponding. In compacted soil with few aggregates and little pore space, roots grow poorly and can be cut off from stored water and nutrients. Clay, adsorbed calcium and magnesium, and iron oxides act as cementing agents, while exchangeable sodium lowers stability by promoting dispersion. Tillage, machinery traffic and livestock traffic are the main disruptors. Reduced or zero tillage, cover crops, perennial crops and organic inputs improve aggregation, whereas heavy or irregular rainfall, and warmer temperatures that speed decomposition and carbon loss, can lower it. See also {{ref:soil-phys-005}}.

soil-phys-039.title: Tilth: what makes soil fit for a crop
soil-phys-039.text: By one 2021 estimate, tillage turns 1840 km3 of soil a year worldwide, against 960 km3 moved by plant roots and earthworms. All that plowing chases tilth, the physical condition of a soil, especially how well it suits planting and growing a crop. Soil in good tilth is spongy, with large pores for air and water and a reasonable store of water and nutrients. Its aggregates are strong enough to hold together yet friable, crumbling readily under shallow tilling. Too much strength yields large cemented clods. Tilth depends on stable aggregates, moisture, air and soil life, and it can change quickly. Tillage improves it only briefly, and long-term plowing tends to compact the soil. The most stable tilth comes from life: substances released by roots feed bacteria that secrete sugar chains ({{ref:soil-bio-284}}), and fungi whose hyphae bind particles. Grass and legume sods, deep-rooted perennials such as alfalfa, and cover crops help rebuild compacted soil.

soil-phys-233.title: Cover and rotation crops that loosen packed soil
soil-phys-233.text: Roots can do work that machines cannot. Cover and rotation crops reduce compaction by creating and stabilizing large voids and feeding microbes. Grasses have shallow dense roots that ease surface compaction but not subsoil, while deep main roots such as those of alfalfa and forage radish penetrate compacted subsoil, so mixes of shallow and deep rooters are often best. Perennial and cool-season crops have active early-season roots that reach compacted layers while still wet and soft. Clay soils stay plastic for long because the dry upper inch cuts evaporation; a spring cereal rye cover pumps water from below and helps the soil pass from plastic to friable, instead of fall tillage. Plowing down a crop loosens trafficked soil and speeds nitrogen mineralization, whereas cutting and mulching in no-till gives weed control and better infiltration but does not loosen the soil. This answers {{ref:soil-phys-082}}.

soil-phys-231.title: Preventing surface sealing and crusting
soil-phys-231.text: A rotary hoe can break a soil crust, but the relief lasts only a short time. Crusting is a symptom of aggregate breakdown, so lasting control means protecting the aggregates. The long-term remedies are less or no tillage, residue or mulch on the surface, cover crops and organic matter to raise aggregate stability. Residue covering even 30% of the surface greatly reduces crusting and gives water pathways in. On very unstable soils of the type described in {{ref:soil-chem-009}}, gypsum promotes aggregation: as it dissolves it adds calcium and raises the salt concentration of soil water. For how crusts form, see {{ref:soil-phys-031}}.

soil-agri-011.title: Variable rate application: changing the dose as you go
soil-agri-011.text: A GPS-guided spreader can raise or lower its fertilizer rate as it crosses a field, because nutrient needs differ with soil properties and sunlight. Variable rate application applies a material such as fertilizer at a rate that changes with the location or qualities of each part of a field. It is either map based, following prescription maps an advisor prepares in advance, or sensor based, calculated in real time on the applicator. A sensing method, {{ref:soil-meth-037}}, considered cost-effective and non-destructive, can make the maps. Varying the rates of nutrients or pesticides can cut their use, saving costs and reducing harmful runoff into waterways.

soil-agri-072.title: Strip farming: alternating bands that act as dams
soil-agri-072.text: Where a slope is too steep, or no other method can prevent erosion, farmers turn to strips. Strip farming, also called strip cropping, divides a field into long, narrow strips that alternate in a crop rotation. Strips of close-sown hay, wheat or forage, serving mainly as cover crops, alternate with row crops such as corn, soybeans, cotton or sugar beets. Laid out along the approximate contour, the sod strips act as natural dams. They slow water and hold back soil that runoff would wash from the cultivated strips. Strips are usually 25 feet (7.6 m) to 75 feet (23 m) wide, and 50 feet (15 m) suits most machinery. On the dry-farmed Great Plains and Canadian Prairies, strips run at right angles to the wind. Contour strip cropping, used mainly on gentle slopes, makes the protective strips wider so they intercept runoff. In strip intercropping, narrower contiguous strips suit machinery and let neighboring crops benefit from each other. In the Midwestern United States, strips of native plants, described in {{ref:soil-agri-142}}, serve as contour buffers and edge-of-field filters that build soil health and curb erosion.

soil-agri-170.title: Web Soil Survey: soil maps on demand
soil-agri-170.text: New surveys of the same county once took 30 to 60 years to appear. Web Soil Survey, run by the USDA's {{ref:soil-hist-050}}, ended that wait. US surveys are no longer printed as books. They are published online, holding everything in the old county reports plus extra tools, and can be updated as needed. It gives access to data from the National Cooperative Soil Survey, building on the {{ref:soil-agri-082}} and the {{ref:soil-agri-084}}. A user picks an area of interest anywhere in the United States where survey data exist. The Soil Map tab then shows the component soil map units, and a report can be saved as a PDF. The Soil Data Explorer gives properties for each map unit, such as depth to water table, surface texture, bulk density, pH and depth to a restrictive layer. It also gives suitability ratings, with reasons, for uses such as dwellings with basements, local roads and streets, vegetative productivity and wastewater disposal by irrigation. It is one recognized basis, alongside measured infiltration rates, for choosing the hydrologic soil group of a site.

soil-agri-182.title: Grass cover crops and what they scavenge
soil-agri-182.text: Grass cover crops include annual cereals (rye, wheat, triticale, barley, oats), forage grasses such as ryegrass, and warm-season grasses such as sorghum-sudangrass. Their fibrous root systems scavenge leftover nutrients, especially nitrogen, and some establish rapidly to greatly reduce erosion. They produce large amounts of residue and roots that add organic matter, and the residue helps suppress weed germination. Cereal rye grows in late fall and early spring as a {{ref:soil-agri-068}} and soil conditioner in cool regions. In Maryland it is widely used to cut nutrient loading into the Chesapeake Bay.

soil-agri-189.title: Ending a cover crop: termination methods
soil-agri-189.text: Every cover crop has to stop before the cash crop can thrive. Termination kills or drastically weakens it before or during soil preparation. Methods include mowing after flowering, herbicide with no-till, plowing in, mow-roll-crimp with no-till planting in one pass, and winter injury. Waiting a week or two lets residue decompose, which eases nitrogen immobilization, allelopathy, damping-off, cutworm and wireworm problems, and gives a better bed for the seed. A sudex cover crop is especially allelopathic, so tomatoes, broccoli and lettuce should wait six to eight weeks.

soil-agri-192.title: Crop diversification in time and space
soil-agri-192.text: Diversity can be added to a farm in time, in space, or both. Cover crops and rotations diversify over time; different crops in different fields or strips diversify across the landscape. A staggered rotation gives both. Perennials add diversity with less frequent rotations, as when dairy farmers grow alfalfa three to four years before corn. Growing trees with crops, described in {{ref:soil-agri-140}}, and integrated livestock add further dimensions. Behind all of this sits an ecological principle: diversity contributes to stability and productivity.

soil-agri-221.title: Land use: what people do with a parcel
soil-agri-221.text: Every parcel of land has a job. Land use describes what people do on it, covering the benefits taken from it and the management actions applied. The FAO defines it as the products and benefits obtained from land together with the management actions people carry out to obtain them. The IPCC defines it as the total of arrangements, activities and inputs applied to a parcel, and groups it into forest land, cropland, grassland, wetlands, settlements and other lands. The choices matter for {{ref:soil-found-077}}, water, {{ref:soil-fert-181}}, plants and animals. Poor choices contribute to soil erosion, {{ref:soil-env-058}}, {{ref:soil-env-062}} and {{ref:soil-env-072}}. Arable land was about 10.7% of the land surface in 2015, with 1.3% permanent cropland. Early-1990s figures were 13% arable, 26% pasture and 32% forest and woodland. Governments plan and regulate land use through zoning and other ordinances to avoid land-use conflicts. An urban growth boundary is one such tool.

soil-bio-001.title: The crowded underworld that keeps soil alive
soil-bio-001.text: Soil is home to circa 59% of the world's biodiversity. Soil biology is the study of the activity and ecology of the microbes and animals that live there. Its subject is soil life, also called soil biota or edaphon. That covers every organism that spends a significant part of its life cycle in the soil profile or at the soil-litter interface. The cast runs from bacteria, fungi, {{ref:soil-bio-274}} and {{ref:soil-bio-193}} to earthworms and arthropods. It even includes some snakes and burrowing mammals such as gophers, moles and prairie dogs. These organisms break down {{ref:soil-found-045}}, releasing nutrients for plants. In doing so they strongly shape the soil's fertility, plant growth, soil structure and carbon storage. Soil life powers the nutrient cycles. Without it, organic material would pile up as undecayed litter, with no dark, stable residue formed and no nutrients available to plants. Soil life also guards what it gathers: nitrogen and phosphorus held in its bodies are kept from leaching away. Microbial exudates help hold soil structure together, and earthworms mix the soil as they burrow. For all that, soil biology is a relatively new science with much still unknown. The discovery of {{ref:soil-bio-121}} in 1996 showed that basic questions about how elements cycle through soil remained open.

soil-bio-005.title: Why ecologists treat soil as an ecosystem
soil-bio-005.text: Soil organisms live under constant threat of drying out. Soil ecology studies how they interact with one another and with their environment. It is especially concerned with nutrient cycling, the formation of soil aggregates and {{ref:soil-bio-008}}. Because soil is so complex and internally connected, soil ecologists regard it as an ecosystem in its own right. It is an uneven mix of minerals and soil organic matter, and its variations in structure, nutrients, moisture, temperature and pH support different organisms. Moisture is a major limit, and microbial communities shift through cycles of drying and rewetting. Temperature swings less with depth and governs microbial and enzyme activity, the release of nutrients and the pace of decay. Most soil organisms need oxygen. Microbes grow in air-filled micropores, while larger animals need macropores or water films to move. Patchy soils across a landscape, and changes between horizons, make communities patchy and layered with depth. Yet soil organisms remain underrepresented in studies and models, partly from an assumption that much below-ground diversity is ecologically redundant.

soil-bio-008.title: Five hundred sheep beneath a football pitch
soil-bio-008.text: The organisms living beneath a football pitch are estimated to equal the size of 500 sheep. Soil biodiversity is the relationship between soil and that variety of life, including the aspects of soil that can be managed with it in mind. Soil is chiefly a habitat for microbes such as bacteria and fungi. It also houses tiny animals such as protozoa and {{ref:soil-bio-193}}, small ones such as potworms and {{ref:soil-bio-209}}, and larger ones such as earthworms, termites and millipedes. Their primary role is to recycle dead organic material from the plant-based food web above ground. In turn, their activity is a primary factor in how soil forms, physically and chemically. The link shows on maps: natural and farm vegetation boundaries closely follow soil boundaries, even at continental and global scales. Microbial exudates are now accepted as the main force that binds soil particles into clumps and shields carbon from further breakdown. Soil health depends on this diversity. Living covers on the soil and carbon-containing amendments improve it. {{ref:soil-agri-004}}, {{ref:soil-agri-192}}, legume intercrops and organic inputs all correlate with more diverse soil life.

soil-bio-011.title: Soil microbiology and the 33,000 species on a beet root
soil-bio-011.text: In 2011, researchers detected more than 33,000 bacterial and archaeal species on the roots of sugar beet. Soil microbiology studies such microorganisms: what they do and how they affect soil properties. Its subjects are grouped as bacteria, including cyanobacteria and actinomycetes, archaea, fungi, algae, slime molds and {{ref:soil-bio-274}}. Their history is long. The first cyanobacteria arose two to four billion years ago. They fixed carbon and nitrogen, releasing oxygen into the air and nitrogen into the soil. How diverse a soil's microbes are depends on its pH, texture, soil organic matter content, plant community and contaminants such as heavy metals. That diversity pays off. Microbes make soil nutrients more available to plants, produce growth hormones, stimulate plant immunity and trigger or dampen plant stress responses. A more diverse soil microbiome, the whole community of soil microbes, generally brings fewer plant diseases and higher crop yields. The microbes also signal to one another through soluble metabolites, volatile organic compounds and extracellular polysaccharides. They trade metabolites that support each other's growth. Farmers can encourage them: sowing {{ref:soil-agri-066}} raises microbial activity, improving nitrogen availability, crop nitrogen uptake and yields.

soil-bio-012.title: Actinomycetes: the branching bacteria behind earthy smell
soil-bio-012.text: The sweet, earthy smell of healthy soil comes from volatile metabolites of actinomycetes. These are soil bacteria of the phylum Actinomycetota (formerly Actinobacteria), Gram-positive and rich in guanine and cytosine, many of which grow fungus-like branching mycelia. The order name Actinomycetales recalls that they were long thought to be fungi. Fungi play a similar role, but these bacteria are much smaller and likely fill a different niche. The phylum is one of the dominant bacterial groups, and among {{ref:soil-bio-002}} it includes {{ref:soil-bio-225}}, one of the largest bacterial genera. This genus and its relatives are major contributors to the biological buffering of soils. They decompose the organic matter of dead organisms so plants can take it up anew. They build humus by breaking down cellulose, {{ref:soil-bio-116}} and arthropod chitin. This substance is hard for most organisms to break down and often shields cellulose from decomposition, so splitting its large molecules into smaller pieces matters. Some, such as {{ref:soil-bio-200}}, live symbiotically with plant roots, fixing nitrogen in exchange for some of the plant's sugars. They need plenty of air and a pH between 6.0 and 7.5, but tolerate dry conditions better than most bacteria and fungi. They also yield many antibiotics, among them streptomycin, neomycin, erythromycin and tetracycline, and agricultural compounds such as insecticides, herbicides, fungicides and plant growth promoters.

soil-bio-022.title: Mesofauna, the mites and jumpers of the pore spaces
soil-bio-022.text: Between 0.2 mm and 2 mm long, the soil mesofauna are mostly the tiny jointed-legged animals of {{ref:soil-bio-209}}, such as mites and {{ref:soil-bio-085}}, plus potworms ({{ref:soil-bio-087}}). The springing kind breed fast and live in large populations. They are prey for predatory mites, pseudoscorpions and macrofauna, which makes them pivotal in soil food webs. Mesofauna feed on plant remains, microbes, lichens, spores, pollen and other animals. Their heavy consumption of litter and microbes gives them an important part in the cycling of carbon. They also eat and break down the feces of larger animals, such as earthworm casts. These small animals cannot reshape soil and must use the existing macropores, which makes them very sensitive to compaction. Potworms instead dig galleries. By eating fungal threads and spores, mesofauna help regulate fungal communities, including fungi that partner with roots, both spreading and severing them. Their community make-up reflects environmental differences, so mesofauna are good bioindicators of soil quality. Being sensitive to environmental hazards, they are likely to be harmed by climate change, {{ref:soil-agri-222}} and farming intensification.

soil-bio-057.title: Chemolithotrophy: making a living from minerals in the dark
soil-bio-057.text: Some microbes build living matter in total darkness, from nothing but minerals and gases. {{ref:soil-hist-013}} first characterized their metabolism, chemolithotrophy. In 1887, working with the bacterium Beggiatoa, he discovered the first known form of lithotrophy. In chemolithotrophy a cell gets its energy by oxidizing reduced inorganic compounds such as ammonia, sulfur, ferrous iron or hydrogen. The oxidation is coupled to making ATP, the cell's energy carrier. Electrons taken from the inorganic donor pass into respiratory chains that make ATP. Most chemolithotrophs also fix carbon dioxide, usually through {{ref:soil-hist-149}}, an energetically expensive pathway. The group includes sulfur oxidizers, iron oxidizers, hydrogen oxidizers and the bacteria that turn ammonia into nitrite and nitrite into nitrate. Oxygen is the usual electron acceptor in the best-documented forms. Nitrate and other acceptors are also used, and the list of chemolithotrophs that live without oxygen is growing. Energy yields depend on the fuel. Oxidizing hydrogen sulfide to sulfur gives 50 kcal/mol (210 kJ/mol), while oxidizing sulfur to sulfate gives 150 kcal/mol (627 kJ/mol). On low-energy fuels such as ferrous iron, cells must process large amounts of material for a little energy, which keeps them from thriving in many places. Because this kind of chemosynthesis needs no sunlight, chemolithotrophs can build living material in the dark. Some thrive above 110 degrees Celsius or below pH 2.

soil-bio-083.title: Entomopathogenic nematodes, worms that hunt insects
soil-bio-083.text: Within 24–48 hours of a tiny worm getting inside, an insect is dead. Entomopathogenic nematodes are thread worms that infect and kill only insects, living as parasites inside them. Their targets live in the soil, from the larvae of moths, flies and beetles to adult grasshoppers and crickets. An infective juvenile enters an insect and releases gut bacteria, Xenorhabdus or Photorhabdus, that kill it. After about a week, hundreds of thousands of new juveniles leave the cadaver. Hunting styles differ. Ambushers such as Steinernema carpocapsae wait at the surface for surface insects. Cruisers such as Heterorhabditis bacteriophora hunt deeper, so {{ref:soil-agri-095}} cut the first's numbers but left the second's unchanged. Both groups are used in {{ref:soil-agri-217}}. Together they cut plum curculio populations by as much as 70–90% in northeastern American orchards. They fail against foliage pests, because UV light and drying harm them.

soil-bio-176.title: Ericoid mycorrhiza, the heath plants' nitrogen miners
soil-bio-176.text: On bogs and heathlands, mineral nitrogen is very scarce, yet {{ref:soil-hist-141}} plants thrive there. Ericoid mycorrhiza is part of the reason: a mutualism between those plants, the Ericaceae, and several lineages of mycorrhizal fungi. The fungi form coils inside the epidermal cells of fine hair roots. Each coil, where soil nutrients are traded for plant sugars, works for only a few weeks before degrading. Their enzymes break down complex organic molecules, taking nitrogen even from cellulose, pectin, chitin and the woody compound described in {{ref:soil-bio-116}}. In acidic, slowly decaying litter layers they pass that nitrogen straight to their hosts.

soil-bio-221.title: Metagenomics: reading the DNA of a whole soil
soil-bio-221.text: A single gram of soil holds about 10^9 to 10^10 microbial cells, and roughly one gigabase of sequence. Metagenomics studies all the genetic material from every organism in such a sample, revealing composition, diversity and functional potential. It profiles communities without culturing species, and early environmental gene studies showed that cultivation had missed most microbial diversity. Norman Pace proposed cloning DNA directly from environmental samples in 1985, and his group first reported doing so in 1991. It differs from {{ref:soil-bio-261}}, or {{ref:soil-bio-262}}. That method reads marker genes and shows which taxa are present. The 16S rRNA gene identifies bacteria and archaea, and 18S rRNA or ITS identifies fungi; more similar sequences are taken to mean closer evolutionary relatedness. Metagenomics sequences all the DNA, so it also recovers enzymes and pathways. Functional metagenomics explores plant-microbe interactions and the roles of uncultivated or rare members in nutrient cycling and plant growth. There is a catch. Sampling is uncontrolled, so the most abundant organisms dominate shotgun sequence data. Long-read sequencing of soils in industrial zones showed that chronic heavy metal contamination restructures the soil microbial community. Soil communities are among the most complex known, which makes {{ref:soil-bio-011}}, {{ref:soil-bio-008}} and the {{ref:soil-bio-227}} natural targets.

soil-bio-284.title: Polysaccharides: sugar chains that store and build
soil-bio-284.text: Wood, paper and cotton are all sugar chains. Polysaccharides are large polymers of monosaccharides linked by glycosidic bonds, ranging from linear to highly branched. Storage types include starch, glycogen and galactogen. Structural ones include cellulose, {{ref:soil-bio-232}}, chitin and pectin. Plant structural parts are mostly cellulose; wood is largely cellulose and lignin, while paper and cotton are nearly pure cellulose. Many organisms digest starch to glucose, but few can metabolize cellulose. Some bacteria and protists can, and ruminants and termites use microorganisms to process it. Humans and many animals lack an enzyme for the beta-linkages, so cellulose is indigestible except where gut bacteria supply it. Chitin yields to chitinase enzymes secreted by bacteria, fungi and some plants. Microbes that detect chitin make enzymes that cleave it to simple sugars and ammonia. It is closely related to chitosan, a more water-soluble derivative. Bacteria, fungi and algae often secrete polysaccharides to adhere to surfaces and avoid drying out, and polysaccharide matrices enclose bacterial biofilms. See {{ref:soil-bio-115}} and the {{ref:soil-bio-271}}.

soil-bio-290.title: Why grassland soils are richer than forest soils
soil-bio-290.text: Soils formed under grassland hold more organic matter, distributed deeper, than soils formed under forest. Grassland roots are deep, extensive and turn over quickly. Slow grass fires also add {{ref:soil-fert-050}} that resists degradation. This helps explain why former grassland soils are highly productive. Forests do it differently. Litter piles on the surface, where organic layers often exceed 50% organic matter, but the mineral layers beneath usually contain less than 2%. The root effect is strong in crops too: about 25-40% of a perennial wheatgrass root system dies back each year, adding much more organic matter than annual wheat. See {{ref:soil-found-045}}.

soil-bio-300.title: Living, active and passive: three kinds of organic matter
soil-bio-300.text: Soil organic matter is usefully split into living, active (dead) and passive (very dead, humus) parts, and each serves a different role. Living matter is roots and organisms in spaces between and inside larger aggregates. Active matter is fresh or partly decomposed residue in the same spaces. Passive matter is fragments of dead microbes held on clay and silt, residue inside micro-aggregates, and compounds hard for organisms to use. A soil needs active matter as well as humus. It supplies nutrients, aggregating glues and food for diverse organisms. It is also the part that suffers first. Early losses after cultivating forest or grassland were nearly all the unprotected active part, and that part rises fastest with {{ref:soil-agri-098}}, rotation, cover crops, manure and compost. See {{ref:soil-found-045}}.

soil-bio-304.title: Filling the soil's organic matter sites
soil-bio-304.text: When practices change to favour buildup, organic matter fills protected sites first and then accumulates mainly as free particles until the soil reaches equilibrium. Free mineral surfaces bond with organic matter first. Small aggregates then form around organic particles, and larger aggregates follow, held by mycorrhizal fungi and small roots. Once all bonding sites and small-aggregate sites are filled, the soil is saturated for that management. Extra organic matter stays as lightly protected free particles that decompose fairly quickly. Depleting practices reverse the order: free particles go first, then aggregate-protected matter, leaving matter tightly held on clay and in micro-aggregates. So a depleted soil can gain much more than one already full for its texture and drainage. With clay and poor aeration, upkeep needs less residue than in well-aerated coarse sands, where raising it is hardest. Case 1 degraded soils and case 2 suboptimal soils gain most from {{ref:soil-fert-076}}. Nearly full case 3 soils should protect what they have, perhaps exporting surplus manure to grain farms. The protection itself is described in {{ref:soil-bio-293}}, and the three pools in {{ref:soil-bio-300}}.

soil-form-141.q: Why are clays such abundant weathering products in soils?
soil-form-141.a: Feldspars make up about 60% of the Earth's crust, and hydrolysis turns them into clays such as illite, smectite and kaolinite.

soil-form-167.q: What made the St. Lawrence Lowlands clays unstable after glaciation?
soil-form-167.a: The Champlain Sea left salt-rich clay there, and leaching of the salt plus river incision made it unstable, causing landslides and flows of the wet clay.
